title: The Big Leap
author: Gay Hendricks
subtitle: Break the upper limit. Live in your Zone of Genius.

chapters.title: Preparing for Your Big Leap
items: Identify your Upper Limit Problem — the inner thermostat that caps how much success, love, and joy you let yourself feel.
Watch for self-sabotage right after things go well; that timing is the diagnostic tell.
Ask the governing question daily: “How much love and success can I allow myself to enjoy?”
Map yourself across the four zones: incompetence, competence, excellence, genius.
Treat the Zone of Excellence as the trap it is — comfortable, well-rewarded, and not where you belong.

chapters.title: Making the Leap
items: Name which false belief holds you back: feeling fundamentally flawed, fearing success means disloyalty or abandonment, believing more success is a bigger burden, or fearing you'll outshine others.
Treat each barrier as an old fear, not a present fact.
Trace the belief to its childhood origin, then separate it from your adult reality.
Extend how long you let a good feeling last — push past your usual cutoff on purpose.
Choose expansion consciously each time the old story resurfaces.

chapters.title: Getting Specific
chapters.tag: Spotting the ULP in daily life
items: Catch worry that points to no real, actionable threat — it's an Upper Limit habit, not useful foresight.
Receive compliments and positive energy fully instead of deflecting them.
Audit your integrity breaches: broken agreements and truths left unspoken.
Recognize blame and criticism as ways you dump good energy.
Notice manufactured arguments, illnesses, and accidents that follow your highs.
Speak the significant truths you've been withholding.

chapters.title: Building a New Home in Your Zone of Genius
items: Answer the four questions: what you most love to do, what doesn't feel like work, what gives the highest results-to-effort ratio, and what your unique ability is.
Pin down your unique ability — the specific thing only you do best.
Reallocate time away from excellence activities toward genius ones.
Keep “wondering” as an open-ended practice rather than forcing a fast answer.
Commit to genius as a way of being, not a weekend hobby.

chapters.title: Living in Your Zone of Genius

mantra.label: Ultimate Success Mantra
mantra.text: I expand in abundance, success, and love every day, as I inspire those around me to do the same.

items: Deploy the mantra the moment you catch yourself Upper-Limiting.
Frame your growth as inspiring others rather than abandoning or outshining them.
Use it as ongoing course-correction, not a one-time affirmation.

chapters.title: Living in Einstein Time
items: Own that you are where time comes from — stop casting yourself as time's victim.
Drop “I don't have enough time” from your language and your thinking.
Locate where you're avoiding responsibility whenever you feel time-pressured.
Stop persecuting yourself and others over time.
Do more of what you love to expand your felt experience of time.

chapters.title: Solving the Relationship Problem

mantra.label: Ultimate Relationship Mantra
mantra.text: I expand in love and creativity every day, as I inspire those around me to do the same.

items: End the blame game by taking 100% responsibility — not a 50/50 split.
Spot the Upper Limit Problem in relationships: sabotage that kicks in after closeness deepens.
Speak unarguable truths (“I feel…”) instead of accusations (“you always…”).
Make clear agreements and keep them.

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
subtitle: Master the rare skill of focused, distraction-free work

chapters.title: Why Deep Work Matters
items: Recognize that deep, focused work produces rare and valuable output that shallow busywork never can.
Treat your ability to concentrate as a competitive advantage in an economy that rewards mastery and complex skill.
Understand that constant connectivity trains your brain for distraction, eroding your capacity for sustained focus.
Prioritize depth over availability — being reachable is not the same as being productive.
Accept that deep work is increasingly rare precisely because it's hard, making it more valuable to those who pursue it.

chapters.title: The Meaning of Depth
items: Seek flow states in your work, not just leisure, to build a sense of craftsmanship and purpose.
Frame your job like a craftsman frames materials — with focus, care, and pride in the outcome.
Use deep work as a tool for a more meaningful professional life, not just higher output.
Notice how fragmented attention correlates with lower life satisfaction and a feeling of busyness without progress.
Commit to depth as a philosophical stance on how you want to spend your working hours.

chapters.title: Rule 1 — Work Deeply
items: Choose a depth philosophy that fits your life: monastic, bimodal, rhythmic, or journalistic.
Schedule deep work blocks in advance and protect them like unmissable appointments.
Build rituals — fixed location, time, and rules — that signal to your brain it's time to focus.
Leverage grand gestures (changing environment, raising stakes) to psychologically commit to a project.
Involve others structurally — hire support or set boundaries — so your best hours stay uninterrupted.
Execute like a business: set a wildly important goal, track lead measures, and keep a visible scoreboard.

mantra.label: Core Principle
mantra.text: Make deep work the default, not the exception — design your days so it happens automatically.

chapters.title: Rule 2 — Embrace Boredom
items: Train your concentration like a muscle — expect effort and resistance at first.
Resist reaching for your phone during every idle moment; let boredom pass instead of numbing it.
Schedule internet use in blocks rather than allowing constant, reflexive checking.
Practice productive meditation — work through a problem mentally during walks or chores.
Memorize something regularly to strengthen your attention and working memory.

chapters.title: Rule 3 — Quit Social Media
items: Apply the craftsman's approach to tool selection: adopt only what delivers substantial, provable benefits.
Run a 30-day break from optional tools to see what you actually miss versus what you assumed you needed.
Cut any tool whose costs to focus outweigh its marginal benefits to your core goals.
Reject the 'any benefit' mindset that justifies distraction because of some small positive.
Reclaim leisure time deliberately instead of defaulting to passive scrolling.

chapters.title: Rule 4 — Drain the Shallows
items: Audit your calendar and classify each task as deep or shallow to reveal how time actually gets spent.
Cap shallow work (email, meetings, admin) to a fixed portion of your week.
Set a firm shutdown ritual each evening to close open loops and protect downtime.
Say no to low-value commitments that eat into deep work capacity without proportional payoff.
Batch shallow tasks into designated windows so they don't fragment your best hours.
Measure your day in output of depth, not hours logged or messages answered.

mantra.label: Daily Rule
mantra.text: Guard your shallow time fiercely so your deep time stays untouched.

title: Where Good Ideas Come From
author: Steven Johnson
subtitle: Innovation is a network, not a lightning bolt

chapters.title: The Adjacent Possible
items: Map the space of recombinations available right now, not the ideal future state you imagine.
Combine existing tools and parts before inventing new ones from scratch.
Explore one step beyond current knowledge instead of leaping toward a distant vision.
Recognize that every breakthrough opens new doors it couldn't have opened before.
Avoid forcing ideas too early; some doors only appear after others are opened.

mantra.label: Core Principle
mantra.text: Innovation lives at the edge of what's currently possible, not in some distant leap.

chapters.title: Liquid Networks
items: Build environments dense enough for ideas to collide but loose enough to recombine freely.
Seek settings between order and chaos — cities, coffeehouses, coral reefs.
Increase the number of connections between minds, not just the number of minds.
Design spaces that force casual encounters between disciplines and strangers.
Resist isolating your best thinkers; connected mediocrity often outperforms isolated genius.

chapters.title: The Slow Hunch
items: Nurture half-formed ideas over years instead of discarding them for lack of instant clarity.
Keep a written record of tentative connections so hunches don't evaporate.
Revisit old notebooks and drafts; today's context can complete yesterday's insight.
Collide multiple slow hunches from different projects to spark a breakthrough.
Protect unfinished ideas from premature judgment or deadline pressure.

chapters.title: Serendipity
items: Wander deliberately through unrelated fields, books, and conversations.
Follow tangents that seem irrelevant; they often carry the real insight.
Diversify your information diet to increase the odds of unexpected collisions.
Talk to people outside your specialty on a regular schedule, not just at conferences.
Create shared physical or digital spaces where unrelated ideas can bump into each other.

mantra.label: Reminder
mantra.text: Chance favors the connected mind — engineer more surface area for luck.

chapters.title: Error & Exaptation
items: Treat mistakes as raw material for new directions, not failures to hide.
Repurpose tools, features, or ideas built for one use into an unrelated function.
Scan your own past failures for latent value under new conditions.
Tolerate noise and inefficiency in early experimentation; clean systems kill surprise.
Ask 'what else could this be used for?' whenever a project stalls.

chapters.title: Platforms
items: Build foundational tools that others can stack unexpected innovations on top of.
Share your infrastructure openly rather than hoarding it for competitive edge.
Study how ecosystems (coral reefs, cities, the web) generate value through openness.
Layer your own work on existing platforms instead of rebuilding basics.
Favor open, connected systems over closed, protected ones for long-term innovation.

mantra.label: Closing Principle
mantra.text: The best innovations don't just solve problems — they become platforms for the next wave of ideas.

title: Never Split The Difference
author: Chris Voss
subtitle: Negotiate like your life depends on it

chapters.title: The New Rules
items: Abandon rational compromise as the goal; treat negotiation as an information-gathering process, not a battle of logic.
Assume emotions drive every decision, then use tactical empathy to steer them.
Listen harder than you talk; silence reveals more than persuasion.
Reject splitting the difference — it often produces a bad outcome for both sides.
Prepare for irrational behavior; treat the other side as unpredictable, not evil.

chapters.title: Be a Mirror
items: Repeat the last three words your counterpart said to prompt them to elaborate.
Slow your voice down and use a calm, late-night FM DJ tone to defuse tension.
Pause after mirroring — let silence pull out more information.
Match body language and tone subtly to build unconscious trust.
Avoid interrogative questions early; mirrors feel safer than direct asks.

chapters.title: Label Emotions, Don't Feel Them
items: Name the emotion you observe — 'It seems like...' or 'It sounds like...' — without judgment.
Diagnose the other side's fears and needs before proposing solutions.
Stay detached from your own emotional reaction to negotiate clearly.
Accusation-audit yourself: list every negative thing they could say about you and say it first.
Validate feelings to lower defensiveness, even if you disagree with the position.

mantra.label: Core Principle
mantra.text: Label the fear before it controls the room.

chapters.title: Beware 'Yes' — Master 'No'
items: Invite 'no' early — it makes people feel safe and in control.
Distinguish counterfeit yes, confirmation yes, and commitment yes; aim only for the last.
Ask 'Is now a bad time to talk?' instead of pushing for immediate agreement.
Reframe rejection as the start of dialogue, not the end.
Use 'How am I supposed to do that?' to make demands feel impossible without saying no.

chapters.title: Trigger 'That's Right'
items: Summarize their situation so accurately they respond with 'that's right,' signaling real alignment.
Avoid 'you're right' — it's dismissive, not agreement.
Reflect their story back using their own words and priorities.
Test understanding by paraphrasing before proposing terms.
Build momentum from small agreements toward the larger deal.

chapters.title: Bend Reality & Bargain Hard
items: Anchor emotionally first, then set an extreme anchor number to skew the range.
Deploy the Ackerman model — start at 65%, then 85%, 95%, and 100% of target with decreasing increments.
Ask calibrated 'how' and 'what' questions to make them solve your problem.
Guarantee follow-through using the Rule of Three — get them to confirm commitment three times.
Hunt for Black Swans — unknown unknowns that can flip the entire negotiation.
Use odd, specific numbers to seem carefully calculated and credible.

mantra.label: Endgame
mantra.text: The best deals come from unearthing what they haven't told you yet.

chapters.title: The Anatomy of Attention
items: Distinguish top-down effortful focus from bottom-up automatic reactions.
Recognize that willpower is a finite mental muscle that depletes with overuse.
Protect deep-focus blocks from the constant pull of digital interruptions.
Notice when your mind wanders and gently redirect it—this is the core rep of attention training.
Understand that selective attention filters an overwhelming world into usable information.

mantra.label: Triad of Focus
mantra.text: Excellence rests on three lenses: awareness of self, empathy for others, and understanding of the wider systems you operate in.

chapters.title: Self-Awareness: Inner Focus
items: Tune into bodily signals and gut feelings before making key decisions.
Label emotions accurately in the moment instead of letting them run unchecked.
Reflect daily on what triggered your strongest reactions and why.
Separate your authentic values from inherited or reactive impulses through quiet self-check-ins.
Use self-awareness as the sensor system that feeds every other focus skill.

chapters.title: Self-Management: Mastering Distraction
items: Delay gratification by rehearsing the 'cool' long-term goal over the 'hot' immediate impulse.
Build routines and environments that reduce the need for constant willpower.
Practice mindfulness meditation to strengthen the neural circuits of sustained attention.
Interrupt rumination loops by shifting attention deliberately to a neutral anchor like breath.
Schedule recovery periods to replenish depleted cognitive control.

chapters.title: Empathy: Other Focus
items: Practice cognitive empathy by actively imagining another person's perspective.
Read nonverbal cues—tone, posture, micro-expressions—to sense unspoken emotions.
Listen fully without planning your response, giving complete attention to the speaker.
Calibrate empathic concern so it drives helpful action rather than emotional overwhelm.
Develop social attunement as the base skill for teamwork, negotiation, and leadership.

chapters.title: Systems Awareness: Outer Focus
items: Zoom out regularly to see how your actions ripple through larger systems and networks.
Question short-term incentives that ignore long-term systemic consequences.
Map the invisible interdependencies—economic, ecological, organizational—that shape outcomes.
Anticipate unintended effects before implementing large-scale decisions.
Cultivate big-picture thinking as a counterbalance to narrow, reactive focus.

chapters.title: Leading with Focus
items: Model the triad of focus—self, others, systems—for those you lead.
Prioritize ruthlessly, protecting attention for what truly matters strategically.
Coach teams to strengthen their own attentional discipline, not just deliver results.
Balance deep focus work with open awareness to catch emerging opportunities and risks.
Design organizational culture that values sustained attention over constant reactivity.
